what: Introduction: Biostatistical Interoperability Between R and SAS
title: 05. R to SAS I/O and Advanced Survival Workflows: Counting Process, Clustering, and Stratification
text: regulated clinical biostatistics, collaborative workflows R SAS essential: Data Exchange: Analysis Data Model (ADaM) Tabulation (SDTM) datasets archived proprietary SAS format (.sas7bdat) SAS transport format (.xpt), yet statistical analysts frequently prototype, explore, visualize using R. Complex Longitudinal Dynamics: Real clinical trials follow subjects multiple visits, generating counting-process start/stop intervals (tstart, tstop, status). Modeling repeated events, time-dependent covariates, multi-center cluster designs requires rigorous variance estimation. Clustered Robust Sandwich Variance: counting-process data, multiple observation rows originate patient. Without clustered robust sandwich standard errors (COVS(AGGREGATE)\text{COVS(AGGREGATE)} SAS, cluster(id) / id = id R), model-based standard errors deflated, leading false-positive statistical significance. Survival Curve Estimation: Estimating adjusted survival probabilities presence time-varying coefficients presents significant challenges: standard baseline estimators (PROC PHREG BASELINE SAS default survfit() R) assume time-invariant relative hazards fail compound time-varying hazard rates correctly. vignette serves operational reference biostatisticians, statistical programmers, validation teams covering: @sec-part1 : Bidirectional Data /O: Reading writing .sas7bdat, .xpt, interchange data preserving column metadata variable labels. @sec-part2 : Counting Process Data Splitting: Expanding survival follow-discrete risk intervals R (survSplit) SAS (%cpdata). @sec-part3 : Multi-Center Clinical Benchmark (survival::cgd): Validating clustered robust sandwich standard errors (id = id) multi-center stratified baseline hazards (strata(center)) TempleCBE SAS PROC PHREG. @sec-part4 : Time-Varying Coefficients & Adjusted Survival: Modeling non-proportional hazards estimating adjusted survival curves using Rossi recidivism cohort via SAS %coxtvc R survfit(..., individual = TRUE). Build validated SAS macro library compile permanent catalogs (sasmacr.sas7bcat). Import macros existing organizational SAS macro libraries (via autocall SASAUTOS= SASMSTORE=). Author, test, register new features local macro library automated batch execution R. @sec-part6 : Joint Modeling Longitudinal & Survival Processes: Auditing repeated measures via proc_contents(..., subject_id = ...) contrasting multi-paradigm predictive modeling (joint_model()) SAS %JM macro (Rizopoulos 2010, Garcia-Hernandez & Rizopoulos 2018). @sec-part7 : Master Macro Catalog & Translation Cheat Sheet: Comprehensive reference mapping SAS syntax TempleCBE.

title: 05. R to SAS I/O and Advanced Survival Workflows: Counting Process, Clustering, and Stratification
text: TempleCBE, pipe-friendly function tidy_tmerge_cox() builds start–stop survival intervals (tstart, tstop, event, event_label) repeated measurement tables, event/censoring tables, baseline covariate tables according standard clinical data registry guidelines:
code: # 1. Load the reference wide tumor dataset (Example 85.7) w <- tumor_wide()  # 2. Reshape wide longitudinal measurements P1..P15 to a tidy measurement frame # The 15 distinct observation/death times in SAS Example 85.7: tt <- c(27, 34, 37, 41, 43, 45, 46, 47, 49, 50, 51, 53, 65, 67, 71)  measure_list <- list() for (i in seq_len(nrow(w))) {   id_i <- w$ID[i]   tm_i <- w$Time[i]   p_vals <- as.numeric(w[i, paste0("P", 1:15)])   # Baseline measurement at time 0 (P1)   measure_list[[length(measure_list) + 1]] <- tibble(ID = id_i, time = 0, NPap = p_vals[1])   # Longitudinal transitions: covariate for interval (tt[k], tt[k+1]] is P[k+1]   for (k in 1:14) {     if (tt[k] < tm_i && !is.na(p_vals[k + 1])) {       measure_list[[length(measure_list) + 1]] <- tibble(ID = id_i, time = tt[k], NPap = p_vals[k + 1])     }   } } measure_df <- bind_rows(measure_list) %>% distinct(ID, time, .keep_all = TRUE)  event_df <- w %>%   select(ID, Time, Dead) %>%   rename(event_time = Time, event_type = Dead)  baseline_df <- w %>%   select(ID, Dose)  # 3. Construct start/stop counting-process intervals via tidy_tmerge_cox tumor_tidy <- tidy_tmerge_cox(   measure_df   = measure_df,   event_df     = event_df,   baseline_df  = baseline_df,   id           = "ID",   measure_time = "time",   event_time   = "event_time",   event_type   = "event_type",   post_event   = "exclude" ) %>%   # Assign event status based on event_type (1 = Dead, 0 = Censored)   mutate(Status = as.numeric(event) * as.numeric(event_type))  cat("tidy_tmerge_cox created", nrow(tumor_tidy), "clinical visit intervals across", length(unique(tumor_tidy$ID)), "subjects.\n") #> tidy_tmerge_cox created 412 clinical visit intervals across 45 subjects. head(tumor_tidy %>% select(ID, tstart, tstop, Status, Dose, NPap), 6) #> # A tibble: 6 × 6 #>      ID tstart tstop Status  Dose  NPap #>   <int>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1     1      0    27      0     1     0 #> 2     1     27    34      0     1     5 #> 3     1     34    37      0     1     6 #> 4     1     37    41      0     1     8 #> 5     1     41    43      0     1    10 #> 6     1     43    45      0     1    10

what: Compressing Consecutive Unchanged Intervals with cumsum()
title: 05. R to SAS I/O and Advanced Survival Workflows: Counting Process, Clustering, and Stratification
text: reproduce exact compressed 102-row table output SAS’s (pp[_i_] ^= qq[_i_]) logic, can collapse contiguous runs unchanged NPap within subject:
code: # Why cumsum()? # 1. lag(NPap) retrieves the covariate value of the previous interval. # 2. NPap != lag(NPap) evaluates to TRUE (1) only when NPap changes, and FALSE (0) otherwise. # 3. default = first(NPap) - 1 guarantees that the initial interval for each ID evaluates to TRUE. # 4. cumsum() calculates the cumulative sum of transitions: each change increments the group ID, #    forming contiguous blocks of unchanged covariate periods per subject. tumor_tidy_compressed <- tumor_tidy %>%   arrange(ID, tstart) %>%   group_by(ID, block = cumsum(NPap != dplyr::lag(NPap, default = dplyr::first(NPap) - 1))) %>%   summarise(     T1 = min(tstart),     T2 = max(tstop),     Status = max(Status),     Dose = dplyr::first(Dose),     NPap = dplyr::first(NPap),     .groups = "drop"   ) %>%   select(ID, T1, T2, Status, Dose, NPap)  cat("Compressed intervals:", nrow(tumor_tidy_compressed), "rows (matching SAS Tumor1 exactly).\n") #> Compressed intervals: 102 rows (matching SAS Tumor1 exactly).

text: R, equivalent approach supplies complete trajectory intervals survfit() using id argument identify single-subject trajectory. Note individual = TRUE argument deprecated survival ≥ 3.2-3 trigger warning current versions:
code: # 1. Define time-varying coefficient interaction on counting process data toy_split$lt_age <- toy_split$age * log(toy_split$time1)  # 2. Fit Cox model with time-varying coefficient fit_tv <- coxph(   Surv(time0, time1, death) ~ female + age + lt_age,   data = toy_split,   ties = "breslow" )  summary(fit_tv)$coefficients #>              coef exp(coef)  se(coef)          z  Pr(>|z|) #> female  1.6422699 5.1668848 2.8381173  0.5786477 0.5628269 #> age    -1.2568579 0.2845467 1.4676221 -0.8563907 0.3917817 #> lt_age  0.1755235 1.1918699 0.5451421  0.3219774 0.7474698  # 3. Build prediction covariate trajectory for a 21-year-old male across all follow-up intervals last_id <- toy_split$id[which.max(toy_split$time1)] target_intervals <- toy_split %>%   filter(id == last_id) %>%   select(time0, time1, death)  pred_trajectory <- data.frame(   age    = 21,   female = 0,   target_intervals ) pred_trajectory$lt_age <- pred_trajectory$age * log(pred_trajectory$time1) pred_trajectory$subj <- 1L # single-subject trajectory; id= requires a grouping column  # 4. Generate adjusted survival curve compounding time-varying hazard contributions per interval # (individual = TRUE was deprecated in survival >= 3.2-3; use id= instead) surv_est <- survfit(fit_tv, newdata = pred_trajectory, id = subj) summary(surv_est) #> Call: survfit(formula = fit_tv, newdata = pred_trajectory, id = subj) #>  #>  time n.risk n.event survival std.err lower 95% CI upper 95% CI #>     1      6       1   0.9625  0.0912     7.99e-01            1 #>     7      4       1   0.8798  0.2199     5.39e-01            1 #>    10      3       1   0.7188  0.3842     2.52e-01            1 #>    13      1       1   0.0815  0.4138     3.91e-06            1

what: Large-Scale Case Study: The Rossi Recidivism Cohort
title: 05. R to SAS I/O and Advanced Survival Workflows: Counting Process, Clustering, and Stratification
text: Rossi recidivism study followed 432 released convicts 52 weeks assess whether financial aid (fin) reduced rearrest (arrest = 1). Prior research demonstrated effect financial aid strongest weeks 20 30, age showed decreasing hazard effect time: coefficient fin_mid strongly protective (HR≈0.23,p=0.029\text{HR} \approx 0.23, p = 0.029), demonstrating financial support significantly lowered recidivism risk critical transition period weeks 20 30.
code: # 1. Load data rossi <- rossi_data("csv")[, 1:10] rossi$id <- seq_len(nrow(rossi))  # 2. Split data at unique arrest weeks (generating 19,805 intervals) cut_rossi <- sort(unique(rossi$week[rossi$arrest == 1])) rossi_split <- survSplit(   data  = rossi,   cut   = cut_rossi,   end   = "week",   start = "week0",   event = "arrest" )  cat("Rossi Split Cohort:", nrow(rossi_split), "start/stop intervals.\n") #> Rossi Split Cohort: 18766 start/stop intervals.  # 3. Create time-varying interactions: #    - age_week: age * week (continuous decay) #    - fin_mid:  financial aid effect specifically between weeks 20 and 30 rossi_split$age_week <- rossi_split$age * rossi_split$week rossi_split$fin_mid <- rossi_split$fin * (20 < rossi_split$week & rossi_split$week < 30)  # 4. Fit multivariable time-varying Cox model with clustering on inmate id fit_rossi_tvc <- coxph(   Surv(week0, week, arrest) ~ age + fin + prio + age_week + fin_mid,   data = rossi_split,   id = id,   ties = "breslow" )  # Model summary table tidy_rossi <- broom::tidy(fit_rossi_tvc, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) tidy_rossi %>%   select(term, estimate, std.error, p.value, conf.low, conf.high) #> # A tibble: 5 × 6 #>   term     estimate std.error  p.value conf.low conf.high #>   <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> #> 1 age         1.03    0.0392  0.417      0.956      1.11  #> 2 fin         0.852   0.205   0.436      0.570      1.27  #> 3 prio        1.10    0.0273  0.000337   1.05       1.16  #> 4 age_week    0.996   0.00146 0.00919    0.993      0.999 #> 5 fin_mid     0.234   0.665   0.0288     0.0635     0.860

text: build validated SAS macro library: Always declare internal macro variables %local prevent namespace collisions. Check required parameters using %%superq(param) = %%; ... %end; (%superq performs macro-quoting blank-check safely handles undefined special-character parameters without triggering resolution errors). Clean intermediate work tables proc datasets lib=work nolist; delete ...; quit;. Place macro .sas file matching macro name lowercase (e.g., cbe_brier_score.sas, cbe_cox_phreg.sas, coxtvc.sas, cpdata.sas). Maintain master loader file (cbe_macros.sas) can initialize whole suite. high-performance enterprise deployments, SAS macros can compiled permanent macro catalog: generates sasmacr.sas7bcat C:\ClinicalTrials\MacroLibrary. Users can execute %cbe_brier_score SAS session simply pointing sasmstore directory without re-compiling.
code: #| lst-label: lst-macro-compile-catalog #| lst-cap: "SAS: Compile and store macros into a permanent catalog (sasmacr.sas7bcat)" /* Compile and store macros permanently into a catalog */ libname mymaclib "C:\ClinicalTrials\MacroLibrary"; options mstored sasmstore=mymaclib;  %macro cbe_brier_score(...) / store source des="TempleCBE IPCW Brier Score & IBS";    /* Macro implementation code */ %mend cbe_brier_score;

what: Joint Modeling of Longitudinal and Time-to-Event Processes (R joint_model vs. SAS %JM Macro)
title: 05. R to SAS I/O and Advanced Survival Workflows: Counting Process, Clustering, and Stratification
text: clinical biostatistics, longitudinal biomarkers (CD4 counts HIV tumor marker trajectories oncology) frequently tracked alongside primary survival endpoints. traditional practice, analysts often fit naive time-dependent Cox regression models: hi(t)=h0(t)exp⁡(β1drugi+β2yi(t))h_i(t) = h_0(t) \exp\left(\beta_1 \text{drug}_i + \beta_2 y_i(t)\right) treating observed biomarker yi(t)y_i(t) piecewise step-function via tmerge %cpdata. However, shown Rizopoulos (2010, JSS 35(9)) Garcia-Hernandez & Rizopoulos (2018, JSS 84(12)), naive time-dependent Cox regression suffers two critical flaws: 1. Measurement Error: Endogenous biological markers recorded laboratory noise. Treating error-free covariates biases hazard ratios toward null (attenuation bias). 2. Informative Dropout & Censoring: Patients worse health trajectories drop experience events earlier, creating informative intermittent missingness. [!IMPORTANT] TempleCBE::joint_model() multi-paradigm prediction framework (penalized Cox + calibrated logistic + duration regression). addresses biases pragmatically regularization , bagged-tree engine, ensemble methods, architecturally distinct full shared-parameter joint models Rizopoulos (2010) Garcia-Hernandez & Rizopoulos (2018), estimate shared latent biological trajectory association parameter (α\alpha) via maximum likelihood (PROC NLMIXED). Section 6.3 contrasts paradigms side--side.

title: 03. Visualizing Computational Pipeline Dependencies
text: TempleCBE’s compute graph architecture fundamentally file-system artifact-oriented, metadata-rich, non-intrusive. Rather acting heavy execution engine R expressions, serves lightweight, human-interpretable dependency auditor visual communication layer: File-system nodes vs. -memory objects: targets, target usually R variable intermediate data frame stored private cache. TempleCBE, every node tangible file disk (FilePath), inspectable anyone using standard file browsers command-line tools. Zero-rewrite adoption vs. Functional refactoring: Adopting targets demands modularizing analysis scripts pure functions writing central _targets.R configuration. contrast, TempleCBE requires zero source code changes: wrap existing project scripts, templates, raw data files, outputs lightweight metadata manifest without touching single line existing analysis code. Language & format agnosticism: targets can track external files via format = "file" Quarto reports via tar_quarto(), primarily R execution engine. TempleCBE treats files equally: raw .xlsx clinical coordinator, .sas data step, .py preprocessing script, .qmd Quarto document, rendered .pdf .docx deliverable first-class nodes. Domain-aware clinical semantics: targets nodes carry computational statuses (e.g. uptodate, queued, running). TempleCBE nodes carry domain-meaningful metadata: workflow lifecycle milestones (stage), semantic analytical roles (artifact_role: raw data, derived baseline data, imputed data, helper scripts, deliverable reports), modification timestamps (mtime), plain-language descriptions. Decoupled execution vs. Monolithic runner: targets tightly couples dependency analysis execution via tar_make(). TempleCBE decouples staleness planning (get_render_plan()) execution: answers stale topological order must rendered, leaving execution mechanics entirely analyst (e.g. Quarto CLI, RStudio, GNU Make, custom batch scripts). Multi-tier stakeholder communication: targets provides developer diagnostics (tar_visnetwork()), TempleCBE provides rich, publication-ready client-ready deliverables: zoomable HTML widgets rich tooltips, neighborhood ego-subgraphs, custom Sugiyama-layout static PNGs, collapsed stage-level diagrams.

text: production biostatistical pipelines collaborative studies (modeled architecture used across CBE studies TempleCBE), best practice encapsulate entire project dependency structure centralized orchestration script named MakeComputeGraph.R. Rather hardcoding ad-hoc graphs interactive sessions, MakeComputeGraph.R provides single source truth entire study lifecycle: Configures study stages & visual identity: Uses pipeline_config() establish human-readable labels color coding every analytical phase. Declares raw & derived assets: Uses FilePath() semantic roles (raw_data, derived_data) analysts know files source registries vs. derived caches. TempleCBE ships exact architecture vignettes/MakeComputeGraph.R (inst/scripts/MakeComputeGraph.R), orchestrating four analytical vignettes: script run, calling pipeline_summary() resulting pipeline immediately yields structured governance audit across project stages: can also use list_stage_data_artifacts() scan directories catalogue derived data files automatically:
code: library(TempleCBE) library(dplyr)  make_temple_compute_graph <- function() {   # 1. Project Pipeline Configuration   pipeline_config(     study_name = "TempleCBE Biostatistical & Survival Analysis Architecture",     stage_labels = c(       "01_EDA"            = "Exploratory Data Analysis & Quality Audit",       "02_Survival_CV"    = "Penalized Coxnet & Nested Cross-Validation",       "03_Compute_Graph"  = "Pipeline Dependency & Governance Graph",       "04_SAS_Validation" = "SAS PROC PHREG Benchmark Validation"     ),     stage_colors = list(       "01_EDA"            = "#DDEBF7",       "02_Survival_CV"    = "#FCE4D6",       "03_Compute_Graph"  = "#E8DAEF",       "04_SAS_Validation" = "#D4EFDF"     )   )    # 2. Raw Data Inputs   raw_clinical <- FilePath(     name = "raw_patient_registry",     path = "data/raw/patient_registry.csv",     renders = FALSE,     stage = "01_EDA",     artifact_role = "raw_data",     description = "Raw clinical intake data with missing biomarker measurements"   )    sas_benchmark_raw <- FilePath(     name = "tumor_wide_data",     path = "data/raw/Tumor.xlsx",     renders = FALSE,     stage = "04_SAS_Validation",     artifact_role = "raw_data",     description = "45-animal longitudinal papilloma count study (SAS Example 85.7)"   )    # 3. Stage 01: EDA & Missingness Analysis   cleaned_cohort_rds <- FilePath(     name = "cleaned_cohort_rds",     path = "data/derived/cleaned_cohort.rds",     renders = FALSE,     stage = "01_EDA",     artifact_role = "derived_data",     description = "Audited and normalized clinical cohort"   )    eda_report <- create_qmd_renderer(     name = "01_eda_and_missingness",     path = "vignettes/eda_and_missingness.Rmd",     deps = list(raw_clinical),     file_stage = "01_EDA",     description = "Missingness auditing, outlier fences, and feature normalization"   )   eda_report@output <- c(eda_report@output, list(cleaned_cohort_rds))    # 4. Stage 02: Penalized Coxnet & Nested Cross-Validation   survival_cv_report <- create_qmd_renderer(     name = "02_nested_survival_cv",     path = "vignettes/nested_survival_cv.Rmd",     deps = list(cleaned_cohort_rds),     file_stage = "02_Survival_CV",     description = "Subject-grouped nested cross-validation and elastic-net Cox modeling"   )    # 5. Stage 04: SAS Validation & Time-Dependent Covariates   tumor_cp_rds <- FilePath(     name = "tumor_counting_process_rds",     path = "data/derived/Tumor1.rds",     renders = FALSE,     stage = "04_SAS_Validation",     artifact_role = "derived_data",     description = "Start/stop counting-process records generated via tidy_tmerge_cox"   )    sas_report <- create_qmd_renderer(     name = "04_sas_survival",     path = "vignettes/sas_survival.Rmd",     deps = list(sas_benchmark_raw),     file_stage = "04_SAS_Validation",     description = "Numerical validation against SAS PROC PHREG and tidy start/stop merging"   )   sas_report@output <- c(sas_report@output, list(tumor_cp_rds))    # 6. Stage 03: Compute Graph & Governance   graph_report <- create_qmd_renderer(     name = "03_compute_graph",     path = "vignettes/compute_graph.Rmd",     deps = list(eda_report, survival_cv_report, sas_report),     file_stage = "03_Compute_Graph",     description = "Dependency graph auditing, staleness detection, and pipeline governance"   )    # Assemble full pipeline   list(     raw_clinical,     sas_benchmark_raw,     eda_report,     cleaned_cohort_rds,     survival_cv_report,     sas_report,     tumor_cp_rds,     graph_report   ) } mcg_path <- if (file.exists("MakeComputeGraph.R")) {   "MakeComputeGraph.R" } else if (file.exists("vignettes/MakeComputeGraph.R")) {   "vignettes/MakeComputeGraph.R" } else {   system.file("scripts", "MakeComputeGraph.R", package = "TempleCBE") }  if (nzchar(mcg_path) && file.exists(mcg_path)) {   source(mcg_path)   temple_pipe <- make_temple_compute_graph()   pipeline_summary(temple_pipe) } #> ======================================================================== #>                       Computational Pipeline Summary                     #> ======================================================================== #> Total Nodes: 12 | Total Edges: 12 | Stale Nodes: 6 (Needs Re-render) #>  #> Artifact Roles: #>   - deliverable_report        :  4 #>   - derived_data              :  2 #>   - raw_data                  :  2 #>   - report_source             :  4 #>  #> Pipeline Stages Breakdown: #>              stage Reports Data_Files Helpers Total #>             01_EDA       2          2       0     4 #>     02_Survival_CV       2          0       0     2 #>   03_Compute_Graph       2          0       0     2 #>  04_SAS_Validation       2          2       0     4 #> ======================================================================== # Inspect all data files in an imputation output folder stage_artifacts <- list_stage_data_artifacts(   stage_dir = "data/derived/imputation",   stage = "03_imputation" )

title: 01. Exploratory Data Analysis, Missingness Auditing, and Normalization
text: clinical trials, electronic health records (EHR), epidemiological registries, data cleanliness rarely given. Datasets frequently exhibit complex missingness patterns, non-standard missing codes (e.g. "999", "-99", "Unknown", "Refused", ""), extreme statistical outliers data-entry errors severe disease phenotypes. Standard data science tools often assume missingness cleanly represented NA, requiring destructive multi-pass preprocessing exploratory analysis can even begin. TempleCBE package provides domain-tailored biostatistical tools audit non-standard missingness non-destructively, rank feature completeness, standardize numerical features, classify clinical outliers formal IQR standards, transition seamlessly tuned machine-learning imputation.

what: Existing tools and their limitations in clinical workflows
title: 01. Exploratory Data Analysis, Missingness Auditing, and Normalization
text: naniar & visdat: Pioneered tidy representation visualization missing data (vis_miss(), gg_miss_var()). However, operate exclusively existing NA values. raw clinical data contains sentinel values ("999", "-99", blank strings), users must first apply mutating functions like replace_with_na_all(), can accidentally alter legitimate numerical values, modify factor levels, mutate data types. mice / Amelia: Primarily multiple imputation engines. include basic diagnostics (e.g. md.pattern()), tools oriented toward parameter checking rather automated feature-level reporting regulatory deliverables. Base R / dplyr summaries: Simple calls like colSums(.na(df)) provide quick counts, lack built-percentage calculations, descending order sorting, sentinel code awareness, publication-ready formatting.

title: 01. Exploratory Data Analysis, Missingness Auditing, and Normalization
text: TempleCBE built specifically constraints institutional biostatistics core facilities: Zero-mutation non-standard code auditing: SumNa() features_percent_miss() natively accept vectors custom missing codes (na_list = c("999", "-99", "", "Unknown", "NA")). compute exact missingness counts percentages without altering coercing underlying data frame. Two-tier clinical outlier governance: generic outlier functions often rely simple z-score cutoffs arbitrary quantiles, detect_outliers() implements Tukey’s formal biostatistical standard, explicitly distinguishing MILD (1.5×IQR1.5 \times \text{IQR}) EXTREME (3.0×IQR3.0 \times \text{IQR}) outliers returning structured classification flags preserve patient keys. Controlled imputation benchmarking: add_missing() function allows statisticians simulate controlled Missing Completely Random (MCAR) mechanisms complete datasets, tracking exact row--column coordinates every amputed cell empirically validate downstream imputation performance. Seamless transition tuned imputation: TempleCBE links missingness auditing directly high-performance imputation engines (missforest_sweep_mtry() missranger_sweep_mtry()) automatically optimize random forest hyperparameters (mtry) independently clinical feature.

what: 1. Starting with a Full Synthetic Clinical Cohort
title: 01. Exploratory Data Analysis, Missingness Auditing, and Normalization
text: demonstrate missingness auditing empirically evaluate imputation accuracy, begin relatively full synthetic cohort N=120N = 120 clinical patients. real-world studies, true underlying values unknown lost. generating complete cohort realistic physiological correlations first, establish verifiable ground truth enables downstream recovery benchmarking: dataset contains: - Continuous biomarkers: age, systolic_bp, bmi, cholesterol, glucose. - Categorical clinical factors: smoker, hypertension, disease_stage. - Unique identifier: patient_id.
code: set.seed(2026) n <- 120  # Realistic clinical covariance structure age <- round(rnorm(n, mean = 58, sd = 9)) bmi <- round(rnorm(n, mean = 27.0, sd = 3.8), 1) systolic_bp <- round(95 + 0.45 * age + 0.65 * bmi + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 7)) cholesterol <- round(155 + 0.55 * age + 1.10 * bmi + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 15)) glucose <- round(72 + 0.35 * age + 0.95 * bmi + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 10)) smoker <- factor(sample(c("No", "Yes"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.65, 0.35))) hypertension <- factor(ifelse(systolic_bp >= 135 | (age >= 62 & bmi >= 28), "Yes", "No")) disease_stage <- factor(sample(c("Stage I", "Stage II", "Stage III", "Stage IV"), n,   replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.30, 0.30, 0.25, 0.15) ))  cohort_clean <- tibble::tibble(   patient_id    = sprintf("PT_%03d", seq_len(n)),   age           = age,   systolic_bp   = systolic_bp,   bmi           = bmi,   cholesterol   = cholesterol,   glucose       = glucose,   smoker        = smoker,   hypertension  = hypertension,   disease_stage = disease_stage )  # Preview the clean cohort head(cohort_clean, 6) #> # A tibble: 6 × 9 #>   patient_id   age systolic_bp   bmi cholesterol glucose smoker hypertension #>   <chr>      <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl>   <dbl> <fct>  <fct>        #> 1 PT_001        63         147  34.2         244     133 Yes    Yes          #> 2 PT_002        48         140  35.1         189     134 No     Yes          #> 3 PT_003        59         148  27.9         187     117 No     Yes          #> 4 PT_004        57         146  30.4         200     111 No     Yes          #> 5 PT_005        52         132  20.4         222     128 No     No           #> 6 PT_006        35         129  28.8         219     128 Yes    No           #> # ℹ 1 more variable: disease_stage <fct>  # Verify complete data integrity (zero missingness) SumNa(cohort_clean) #> [1] 0

what: Heterogeneous missingness: Column-specific proportions via vector pct_na
title: 01. Exploratory Data Analysis, Missingness Auditing, and Normalization
text: real-world clinical cohorts, different variables rarely share identical missingness rate. Routine clinical covariates (age bmi) may missing 5–10% records, whereas specialized laboratory panels (cholesterol glucose) may uncollected 25–35% patients. add_missing() supports numeric vector pct_na whose length matches number selected columns: Notice features_percent_miss() directly reflects column’s distinct amputation share, missing_cells attribute accurately tracks varying number masked cells per feature.
code: # Generate column-specific missingness proportions with runif() set.seed(42) cols_ampute <- c("age", "systolic_bp", "bmi", "cholesterol", "glucose", "smoker", "hypertension")  p_vector <- cols_ampute |>   length() |>   runif(min = 0.05, max = 0.30) |>   round(2)  names(p_vector) <- cols_ampute p_vector #>          age  systolic_bp          bmi  cholesterol      glucose       smoker  #>         0.28         0.28         0.12         0.26         0.21         0.18  #> hypertension  #>         0.23  # Amputate each column according to its specific proportion amputed_hetero <- add_missing(   cohort_clean,   cols = c(age, systolic_bp, bmi, cholesterol, glucose, smoker, hypertension),   pct_na = p_vector )  # Inspect how features_percent_miss captures the heterogeneous rates features_percent_miss(amputed_hetero) #> # A tibble: 9 × 5 #>   feature       SumNa SumComp PctNa PctComp #>   <chr>         <int>   <int> <dbl>   <dbl> #> 1 age              34      86 0.283   0.717 #> 2 systolic_bp      34      86 0.283   0.717 #> 3 cholesterol      31      89 0.258   0.742 #> 4 hypertension     28      92 0.233   0.767 #> 5 glucose          25      95 0.208   0.792 #> 6 smoker           22      98 0.183   0.817 #> 7 bmi              14     106 0.117   0.883 #> 8 patient_id        0     120 0       1     #> 9 disease_stage     0     120 0       1

what: The mtry dilemma in clinical data
title: 01. Exploratory Data Analysis, Missingness Auditing, and Normalization
text: Random forest imputation iterates variable missing values, fitting forest predicting variable variables. single impactful hyperparameter mtry — number candidate variables sampled split: - mtry low, strong predictive biomarkers may missed key splits. - mtry high, trees become correlated overfit noisy clinical features. Critically, different clinical variables perform best different mtry values. continuous biomarker (e.g. systolic_bp) may achieve minimal error mtry=3mtry = 3, whereas binary factor (e.g. smoker) may perform best mtry=1mtry = 1. Standard implementations force analysts choose single global mtry.

what: Existing tools and their limitations in longitudinal clinical modeling
title: 02. Penalized Cox Models and Nested Cross-Validation for Start/Stop Survival Data
text: survival (Therneau): foundational baseline semi-parametric Cox proportional hazards Kaplan-Meier estimation. excellent classical low-dimensional epidemiological inference, lacks high-dimensional regularization (lasso, elastic net), automated cross-validation, tidy resampling integration. Data leakage start/stop data: cv.glmnet constructs folds randomly partitioning individual rows. counting-process data (Surv(tstart, tstop, status)), splits intervals belonging patient across training validation folds, leaking patient identity future biomarker trajectory validation set. cluster/site-level grouping: hold entire clinical sites hospital clusters evaluate generalizability across centers. Suboptimal metric selection: chooses penalty parameter λ\lambda using partial likelihood deviance Harrell’s C-index, without support time-dependent calibration, Integrated Brier Scores (IBS), IPCW adjustments. modern formula/recipe preprocessing: Predictors must supplied raw numeric design matrix (xx), forcing manual one-hot encoding outside cross-validation loop. Silent scoring failures: yardstick survival metrics expect one row per subject right-censored truth (Surv(time, event)). provided counting-process intervals (Surv(tstart, tstop, event)), yardstick returns numbers without error, silently treats every interval independent patient, biasing Brier scores ROC AUCs. Missing integrated nested CV penalized Cox: Evaluating regularized Cox models across α\alpha-mixture λ\lambda-penalty grid subject-level IPCW weights requires bespoke orchestration. pec / riskRegression / survAUC: Provide inverse-probability--censoring weights prediction error curves, operate standalone legacy systems decoupled recipes preprocessing tidymodels grammar.

text: Clinical prognostic modeling frequently involves datasets dozens continuous lab values (e.g. creatinine, bilirubin, blood pressure) alongside categorical clinical indicators (e.g. disease stage, smoking status, sex, treatment center). Standard Principal Component Analysis ([recipes::step_pca()]) operates numeric columns; dummy-encoding categorical variables PCA distorts geometric distances binary indicators different variances continuous variables. step_famd() provides native recipes step Factor Analysis Mixed Data (Pagès 2004, implemented via FactoMineR::FAMD): - Continuous variables normalized unit variance. - Categorical variables dummy-coded weighted inversely category frequencies, ensuring variable contributes proportionally regardless number levels. step_famd() integrates directly cv_coxnet() nested_cv_coxnet(), ensuring components learned strictly inside training fold without leakage.
code: library(recipes)  # Define clinical recipe with mixed numeric and categorical predictors mixed_rec <- recipe(surv ~ age + bmi + marker + treatment + site + patient_id, data = sim_data) |>   update_role(patient_id, new_role = "id") |>   # Apply FAMD to compress continuous and discrete predictors into 3 components   step_famd(age, bmi, marker, treatment, site, num_comp = 3, prefix = "FAMD_")  # Train and inspect component contributions prepped_famd <- prep(mixed_rec, training = sim_data) baked_features <- bake(prepped_famd, new_data = NULL) head(baked_features)  # Inspect variance explained by components tidy(prepped_famd, number = 1, type = "variance")

what: Introduction: Dimension Reduction in Clinical and Exploratory Data Analysis
title: 07. Principal Component Analysis in R and SAS
text: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) unsupervised machine learning exploratory data analysis (EDA) technique widely utilized across biostatistics, clinical trials, epidemiological research. analyzing large cohorts extensive clinical measurements—repeated physiological scores, biomarker panels, intensive care metrics—investigators often face high dimensionality severe multicollinearity. summarized biostatistician Darina Chudnovskaya: “put simply, just think principal components new axes provide best angle see evaluate data, differences observations better visible.” — Darina Chudnovskaya (citing builtin.com) PCA reduces dimensionality multivariate continuous datasets transforming correlated variables smaller set uncorrelated, orthogonal variables known Principal Components (PCs). principal component linear combination original variables, structured : 1. first principal component (PC1PC_1) captures maximum possible variance data. 2. subsequent component (PC2,PC3,…PC_2, PC_3, \dots) captures maximum possible remaining variance mathematical constraint orthogonal (uncorrelated) preceding components. 3. total variance across principal components equals total variance original variables. principal components linear combinations may single physical unit measurement, analyzing loadings (eigenvectors) eigenvalues reveals underlying data structures, detects clustering, helps researchers select representative covariates downstream multivariable survival modeling (cbe_cox_multi()).

title: 07. Principal Component Analysis in R and SAS
text: mathematical execution PCA proceeds five fundamental steps: Standardize Variables: PCA sensitive measurement scales (variables larger numerical ranges spuriously dominate variance), features centered mean zero (μ=0\mu = 0) scaled unit variance (σ=1\sigma = 1): zij=xij−x‾jsjz_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij} - \bar{x}_j}{s_j} Standardizing mathematically equivalent performing PCA correlation matrix 𝐑\mathbf{R} rather unscaled covariance matrix 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma}. Calculate Correlation / Covariance Matrix: symmetric p×pp \times p correlation matrix 𝐑\mathbf{R} computed, capturing pairwise linear relationships correlation directions (+1+1 −1-1). Calculate Eigenvalues Eigenvectors: Eigen-decomposition solves characteristic equation: det⁡(𝐑−λ𝐈)=0⟹𝐑𝐯k=λk𝐯k\det(\mathbf{R} - \lambda \mathbf{}) = 0 \quad \implies \quad \mathbf{R} \mathbf{v}_k = \lambda_k \mathbf{v}_k Eigenvalues (λk\lambda_k): Represent variance explained kk-th principal component. standardized PCA pp variables, ∑k=1pλk=p\sum_{k=1}^p \lambda_k = p. Eigenvectors (𝐯k\mathbf{v}_k): Unit-length directional vectors defining principal axes (loadings). Select Principal Components: Kaiser-Guttman Criterion: Retain components eigenvalues λk≥1\lambda_k \ge 1 (explaining variance individual original standardized variable). Scree Plot Elbow: Identify inflection point additional components yield diminishing marginal variance. Cumulative Variance Threshold: Retain enough components explain pre-specified proportion variance (typically 70%–80%). Recast Observations onto Principal Component Axes: Observations projected onto retained eigenvectors generate principal component scores: 𝐘=𝐙𝐕k\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{Z} \mathbf{V}_k

what: Connecting PCA to Multivariable Cox Survival Modeling
title: 07. Principal Component Analysis in R and SAS
text: Darina Chudnovskaya’s applied research, univariable Cox regression showed physiological indicators (tas_baseline, tas_min, tas_max, tas_ave, age) statistically significant predictors survival, whereas length stay metrics (los_icu, los_hosp) primarily reflected post-admission hospital course: Collinearity Identification: tas_min, tas_max, tas_ave cluster tightly loading space. Entering three simultaneously multivariable Cox model (cbe_cox_multi()) inflates variance causes coefficient instability. Dimension Separation: PCA isolates hospital stay duration axis (PC1PC_1) acute physiological thermal volatility (PC2PC_2 PC3PC_3). Model Selection Guidance: conjunction univariable tables (cbe_cox_single()) baseline summaries (my_summary_table()), PCA provides empirical justification retaining single representative metric (tas_ave tas_baseline) constructing orthogonal composite score.

title: 06. Python Interoperability: Validating LOCO-MP Survival Ensembles with reticulate, rpy2, and DataSlingers/LOCOMP
text: Quantifying predictive contribution individual covariates central biomedical discovery, translational biomarker prioritization, regulatory evaluation. Traditional machine learning interpretability methods face substantial limitations: Permutation Feature Importance (PFI): Permuting single feature can create unphysical combinations presence strong collinearity, inflating false-positive discovery. Drop-Column (Retraining) LOCO: Training pp distinct models, omitting one covariate, computationally prohibitive high-dimensional genomic arrays complex survival ensembles. code: """ Python script: Call TempleCBE LOCO-MP Cox model via rpy2 """ import numpy as np import pandas as pd import rpy2.robjects as ro from rpy2.robjects import pandas2ri from rpy2.robjects.packages import importr  # Activate automated Pandas <-> R DataFrame conversion pandas2ri.activate()  # Import TempleCBE and survival packages templecbe = importr('TempleCBE') survival = importr('survival') base = importr('base')  # 1. Load or simulate survival data in Python n = 120 data_py = pd.DataFrame({     'time': np.random.exponential(scale=10, size=n) + 1,     'status': np.random.binomial(1, 0.65, size=n),     'age': np.random.normal(55, 10, size=n),     'biomarker_a': np.random.normal(0, 1, size=n),     'biomarker_b': np.random.normal(0, 1, size=n),     'noise_1': np.random.normal(0, 1, size=n),     'noise_2': np.random.normal(0, 1, size=n) })  # 2. Convert Pandas DataFrame to R DataFrame data_r = pandas2ri.py2rpy(data_py)  # 3. Fit LOCO-MP Penalized Cox Model in TempleCBE fit_r = templecbe.cbe_loco_mp_coxnet(     formula = ro.Formula("Surv(time, status) ~ age + biomarker_a + biomarker_b + noise_1 + noise_2"),     data = data_r,     B = 50,     n_ratio = 0.7,     m_ratio = 0.5,     seed = 42 )  # 4. Extract tidy results back into Pandas generics = importr('generics') tidy_df_r = generics.tidy(fit_r) tidy_df_py = pandas2ri.rpy2py(tidy_df_r)  print("--- TempleCBE LOCO-MP Results in Python ---") print(tidy_df_py[['term', 'importance', 'std_error', 'statistic', 'p_adjusted', 'conf_low', 'conf_high']])

title: 04. Validation and Workflow Guide for SAS Users: Cox Models in TempleCBE
text: Therneau’s survival::tmerge constructs start-stop survival intervals combining baseline cohort data sequential event time-dependent covariate tables: Comparing fitted coefficients tmerge SAS DATA-step Tumor1 data: models identical 10−1710^{-17}! SAS DATA step collapsed adjacent intervals identical values (resulting 102 rows), tmerge splits observation time (resulting 412 rows). hazard risk set contributions intervals unchanged covariates identical, partial likelihood resulting estimates match exactly.
code: # 1. Base cohort with primary follow-up interval and event status base_df <- tumor_wide %>%   select(ID, Time, Dead, Dose)  tumor_tmerge <- tmerge(   data1 = base_df,   data2 = base_df,   id = ID,   Status = event(Time, Dead) ) # 2. Extract longitudinal transitions: at each observation time, update NPap tt <- c(27, 34, 37, 41, 43, 45, 46, 47, 49, 50, 51, 53, 65, 67, 71) transitions <- list() for (r in seq_len(nrow(tumor_wide))) {   id_i <- tumor_wide$ID[r]   tm_i <- tumor_wide$Time[r]   p_vals <- as.numeric(tumor_wide[r, paste0("P", 1:15)])   transitions[[length(transitions) + 1]] <- data.frame(ID = id_i, time = 0, NPap = p_vals[1])   for (k in 1:14) {     if (tt[k] < tm_i && !is.na(p_vals[k + 1])) {       transitions[[length(transitions) + 1]] <- data.frame(ID = id_i, time = tt[k], NPap = p_vals[k + 1])     }   } } tdc_df <- bind_rows(transitions) # 3. Apply time-dependent covariate update via tmerge tumor_tmerge <- tmerge(   data1 = tumor_tmerge,   data2 = tdc_df,   id = ID,   NPap = tdc(time, NPap) ) # proc_compare(tumor_tmerge, Tumor1) # Fit Cox model on tmerge data fit_tmerge <- cbe_cox_multi(   data = tumor_tmerge,   formula = Surv(tstart, tstop, Status) ~ Dose + NPap,   id = ID,   ties = "breslow" ) coef(fit_tmerge$model) #>       Dose       NPap  #> 0.06885124 0.11715304 coef(fit_tumor$model) #>       Dose       NPap  #> 0.06885124 0.11715304  # Difference down to machine precision: max(abs(coef(fit_tmerge$model) - coef(fit_tumor$model))) #> [1] 4.163336e-17

what: Model Calibration & Integrated Brier Score (IBS) Parity
title: 04. Validation and Workflow Guide for SAS Users: Cox Models in TempleCBE
text: clinical risk prediction, model discrimination (Harrell’s CC-index) evaluates relative ordering, fails assess whether predicted absolute probabilities match observed clinical outcomes. Proper scoring rules—specifically Brier score Integrated Brier Score (IBS)—quantify mean squared prediction error right censoring.

previous_headings: Model Calibration & Integrated Brier Score (IBS) Parity
what: Theoretical Foundation: IPCW Brier Score & IBS (Graf et al. 1999)
title: 04. Validation and Workflow Guide for SAS Users: Cox Models in TempleCBE
text: specific evaluation time horizon tt, Brier score measures squared difference true binary survival status (Ti>t)(T_i > t) predicted survival probability Ŝ(t∣Xi)\hat{S}(t \mid X_i). prevent bias censored individuals whose status tt unknown, Graf et al. (1999) weight observations Inverse Probability Censoring Weights (IPCW): BS(t)=1N∑=1Nwi(t)⋅[(Ti>t)−Ŝ(t∣Xi)]2BS(t) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{=1}^N w_i(t) \cdot \left[ (T_i > t) - \hat{S}(t \mid X_i) \right]^2 IPCW weight wi(t)w_i(t) derived Kaplan-Meier estimate censoring distribution Ĝ(u)=P(C>u)\hat{G}(u) = P(C > u): wi(t)={1Ĝ(t),Ti>t(subject remains risk)1Ĝ(Ti−),Ti≤t δi=1(observed event time t)0,Ti≤t δi=0(censored prior time t)w_i(t) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{\hat{G}(t)}, & \text{} T_i > t \quad (\text{subject remains risk}) \\ \frac{1}{\hat{G}(T_i^-)}, & \text{} T_i \le t \text{ } \delta_i = 1 \quad (\text{observed event time } t) \\ 0, & \text{} T_i \le t \text{ } \delta_i = 0 \quad (\text{censored prior time } t) \end{cases} summarize overall model accuracy across entire follow-horizon [tmin,tmax][t_{\min}, t_{\max}], Integrated Brier Score (IBS) integrates time-dependent Brier loss using trapezoidal rule: IBS=1tmax∫0tmaxBS(t)dt≈1tK∑k=1K−1BS(tk)+BS(tk+1)2⋅(tk+1−tk)\text{IBS} = \frac{1}{t_{\max}} \int_0^{t_{\max}} BS(t) \, dt \approx \frac{1}{t_K} \sum_{k=1}^{K-1} \frac{BS(t_k) + BS(t_{k+1})}{2} \cdot (t_{k+1} - t_k)
code: #| lst-label: lst-tumor1-datastep #| lst-cap: "SAS DATA step: Wide-to-counting-process transformation (Tumor1, Example 85.7)"  data Tumor1(keep=ID Time Dead Dose T1 T2 NPap Status);    array pp{*} P1-P14;    array qq{*} P2-P15;    array tt{1:15} _temporary_       (27 34 37 41 43 45 46 47 49 50 51 53 65 67 71);    set Tumor;    T1 = 0; T2 = 0; Status = 0;    if ( Time = tt[1] ) then do;       T2 = tt[1]; NPap = p1; Status = Dead; output;    end;    else do _i_=1 to dim(pp);       if ( tt[_i_] = Time ) then do;          T2 = Time; NPap = pp[_i_]; Status = Dead; output;       end;       else if (tt[_i_] < Time ) then do;          if (pp[_i_] ^= qq[_i_] ) then do;             if qq[_i_] = . then T2 = Time;             else                T2 = tt[_i_];             NPap = pp[_i_]; Status = 0; output;             T1 = T2;          end;       end;    end;    if ( Time >= tt[15] ) then do;       T2 = Time; NPap = P15; Status = Dead; output;    end; run;

what: TempleCBE Implementation on NCCTG Lung Cancer Cohort
title: 04. Validation and Workflow Guide for SAS Users: Cox Models in TempleCBE
text: TempleCBE, survival predictions scored using censoring_km(), add_graf_weights(), yardstick::brier_survival():
code: # Filter complete cases for the multivariable model lung_complete <- lung_data %>%   filter(!is.na(ph.karno))  # 1. Fit multivariable Cox model with Breslow tie handling (matching SAS default) fit_calib <- cbe_cox_multi(   data = lung_complete,   formula = Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.karno,   ties = "breslow" )  # 2. Extract predicted survival curves at milestone evaluation times (100 to 500 days) eval_horizons <- c(100, 200, 300, 400, 500) sfit <- survfit(fit_calib$model, newdata = lung_complete) surv_mat <- summary(sfit, times = eval_horizons)$surv  # Construct per-subject prediction list for yardstick pred_list <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(lung_complete)), function(i) {   tibble::tibble(     .eval_time = eval_horizons,     .pred_survival = surv_mat[, i]   ) })  scored_lung <- tibble::tibble(   .truth = Surv(lung_complete$time, lung_complete$status),   .pred = pred_list )  # 3. Add Inverse Probability of Censoring Weights (IPCW) scored_lung <- add_graf_weights(   scored_lung,   censoring = censoring_km(Surv(lung_complete$time, lung_complete$status)) )  # 4. Compute time-dependent Brier scores and Integrated Brier Score (IBS) brier_res <- yardstick::brier_survival(scored_lung, truth = .truth, .pred) ibs_res <- yardstick::brier_survival_integrated(scored_lung, truth = .truth, .pred)  brier_res #> # A tibble: 5 × 4 #>   .metric        .estimator .eval_time .estimate #>   <chr>          <chr>           <dbl>     <dbl> #> 1 brier_survival standard          100     0.113 #> 2 brier_survival standard          200     0.201 #> 3 brier_survival standard          300     0.230 #> 4 brier_survival standard          400     0.227 #> 5 brier_survival standard          500     0.200 ibs_res #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #>   .metric                   .estimator .estimate #>   <chr>                     <chr>          <dbl> #> 1 brier_survival_integrated standard       0.163

text: verify clinical calibration milestone t=300t = 300 days (near median survival), divide patients predicted survival quintiles compare mean predicted survival observed Kaplan-Meier survival: Calibration 300 days: mean predicted survival versus observed Kaplan-Meier survival within predicted-survival quintiles; dashed line marks perfect calibration.
code: # Extract 300-day predicted survival p300 <- surv_mat[3, ] lung_complete$pred_surv_300 <- p300 lung_complete$quintile <- dplyr::ntile(lung_complete$pred_surv_300, 5)  # Calculate observed Kaplan-Meier within each predicted quintile at t = 300 calib_df <- lung_complete %>%   group_by(quintile) %>%   summarize(     n = n(),     mean_pred = mean(pred_surv_300),     obs_km = {       km <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1)       summary(km, times = 300, extend = TRUE)$surv     },     .groups = "drop"   )  # Calibration plot with 45-degree reference line ggplot(calib_df, aes(x = mean_pred, y = obs_km)) +   geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +   geom_point(aes(size = n), color = "#8B1E41", alpha = 0.85) +   geom_line(color = "#8B1E41", linewidth = 0.8) +   scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.2, 0.9), labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +   scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.2, 0.9), labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +   labs(     title = "Model Calibration at 300 Days (NCCTG Lung Cohort)",     subtitle = "Observed Kaplan-Meier survival vs. Mean predicted survival across risk quintiles",     x = "Mean Predicted Survival Probability",     y = "Observed Kaplan-Meier Survival Rate",     size = "Patients"   ) +   theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +   theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

code: # 1. Prepare R analysis cohort and export to FDA Transport format lung_xpt_data <- lung_data %>%   filter(!is.na(ph.karno)) %>%   rename(ph_karno = ph.karno) %>%   select(time, status, age, sex, ph_karno)  work_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "cbe_sas_job") dir.create(work_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE) xpt_path <- file.path(work_dir, "lung.xpt") driver_path <- file.path(work_dir, "run_brier_macro.sas") out_brier_path <- file.path(work_dir, "sas_brier.sas7bdat") out_ibs_path <- file.path(work_dir, "sas_ibs.sas7bdat")  # Export to standard SAS Version 5 XPORT format (member name <= 8 chars) haven::write_xpt(lung_xpt_data, xpt_path, version = 5, name = "LUNG")  # 2. Dynamically compose SAS driver invoking %cbe_brier_score macro_file <- TempleCBE::cbe_sas_macro_path("cbe_brier_score.sas")  driver_code <- sprintf(' libname workdir "%s"; libname xfile xport "%s";  /* Copy transport file into SAS WORK library */ proc copy in=xfile out=work; run;  /* Include TempleCBE macro */ %%include "%s";  /* Execute macro */ %%cbe_brier_score(     data       = work.lung,     time       = time,     status     = status,     pred_vars  = age sex ph_karno,     eval_times = 100 200 300 400 500,     ties       = BRESLOW,     trunc      = 0.05,     out_brier  = workdir.sas_brier,     out_ibs    = workdir.sas_ibs ); ', gsub("\\\\", "/", work_dir), gsub("\\\\", "/", xpt_path), gsub("\\\\", "/", macro_file))  writeLines(driver_code, driver_path)  # 3. Execute SAS batch job from R status <- TempleCBE::run_sas_script(driver_path) cat("SAS Macro Execution Status:", status, "\n")  # 4. Import SAS output dataset directly back into R sas_brier_tbl <- haven::read_sas(out_brier_path) sas_ibs_tbl <- haven::read_sas(out_ibs_path)  # 5. Display SAS macro results inside R sas_ibs_tbl sas_brier_tbl

Statistical Integrity & Parity: Smoke tests five classic cohorts R’s survival package (veteran, lung, rotterdam, heart, colon) check fits predictions run return well-formed output. SAS parity checked committed reference numbers printed SAS 9.4 PROC PHREG (counting-process tumor data lung cohort), PROC PRINCOMP (eigenvalue table proc_pca() iris), PROC COMPARE (cbe_compare_df() nine small comparisons) IPCW Brier score integrated Brier score macro; re-running SAS opt-(TEMPLECBE_RUN_SAS_TESTS) needs SAS installation. Accelerated Racing Workflows: Integrated finetune ANOVA win-loss racing interfaces (control_race_survival(), tune_race_survival()) fast hyperparameter optimization penalized survival models joint ensembles. Clean Canonical CBE API: Refactored core functions canonical names (km_single, cox_multi, compare_df, etc.) full backwards-compatible cbe_* aliases. Zero-Leakage Assurance: release private list terms must appear checked every tracked file extracted text tracked PDFs (test-denylist.R; runs private list available, release check, part CI).

title: FilePath S4 Class — FilePath-class
text: Represents individual file node computational pipeline dependency graph. FilePath object encapsulates file-level metadata state: tracking modification timestamps (mtime), file extensions (file_ext), workflow lifecycle milestones (stage), semantic pipeline roles (artifact_role), rendering status (renders). Upon instantiation, object automatically inspects target file disk: file exists path, mtime populated file.info()$mtime file_ext extracted via tools::file_ext().

title: FilePath S4 Class — FilePath-class
text: name Character. user-supplied, human-readable name file, used refer file across parts pipeline dependency graph. path Character. absolute project-relative path file file system. mtime POSIXct. modification time file file system. Automatically populated disk object initialization file exists. file_ext Character. file extension file (e.g., "xlsx", "rds", "qmd"). Automatically populated file path object initialization. renders Logical. logical indicating whether file rendered file (.e. file produced rendering process) rendering source script. Defaults FALSE. stage Character. workflow lifecycle stage file pipeline (e.g., "01_EDA", "02_Analysis_Original", "03_Imputation"). artifact_role Character. semantic role file pipeline. Standard roles include: "raw_data": Original immutable input data (e.g. source spreadsheets). "derived_data": Primary processed baseline dataset generated raw inputs. "enhanced_data": Imputed augmented analytical dataset. "intermediate_data": Stage-internal calculation artifact model. "report_source": Executable source document (e.g., Quarto .qmd). "deliverable_report": Rendered deliverable (e.g., .pdf, .html). "helper_script": Child modular helper script invoked parent reports. "reference": Lookup tables, crosswalks, project configuration files. description Character. brief human-readable description file's contents analytical purpose.

title: Pseudonymize Investigator Names (Vectorized) — anonymize_pi
text: Scope. investigator names replaced. Dates, record subject numbers, free text, identifiers left untouched, general de-identification tool; see pi_anonymizer limits. Key required deterministic methods. "hmac_token" "hmac_surname" stop error unless secret key available, key argument TEMPLECBE_SECRET_KEY environment variable. Without secret key anyone can recompute pseudonyms list names. Set variable user .Renviron rather writing key script may committed. Passing allow_default_key = TRUE restores earlier fallback public built-key, warning output secret. check happens data looked , -NA input skip . Methods: "hmac_token" (default): Stateless deterministic token (e.g.,     PI_5c1ebfd9a0b3c4d2) computed via openssl::sha256(name, key = key).     Needs key. mapping file written. "hmac_surname": Stateless deterministic procedural surname generated via     keyed HMAC seed generate_last_names. Needs key. Consistent     across runs without disk state; different names can share surname. "token": Stateful tokens persisted user-level JSON mapping file     (tools::R_user_dir("TempleCBE", "data")/pi_mapping.json), name keeps     token calls. Works without key: new names get random tokens,     exist mapping file. key set, tokens keyed HMAC     name instead. mapping file lists real names next tokens     confidential. function refuses create write inside Git repository     tree, prevent accidental commits. "synthetic": Random procedural surnames via     generate_last_names. Needs key; every element gets new random     surname, repeated names mapped consistently.

title: Pseudonymize Investigator Names (Vectorized) — anonymize_pi
code: # The key comes from the TEMPLECBE_SECRET_KEY environment variable. In real use # keep it in your user ~/.Renviron (see ?pi_anonymizer), never in a script you # commit. Here a throwaway value is set for this example only. if (requireNamespace("withr", quietly = TRUE)) {   withr::with_envvar(c(TEMPLECBE_SECRET_KEY = "example-only-not-a-real-key"), {     # Vectorized deterministic tokens (default method = "hmac_token")     print(anonymize_pi(c("Franklin", "Taylor", "Patel")))      # Short tokens (8 characters)     print(anonymize_pi(c("Franklin", "Taylor"), n_chars = 8))      # Custom renaming function     print(anonymize_pi(c("Franklin", "Taylor"), rename_fn = tolower))      # Vectorized realistic pseudonyms     print(anonymize_pi(c("Franklin", "Taylor"), method = "hmac_surname"))   }) } #> [1] "PI_2713ba3e1fcb5c01" "PI_383a552e8b600d2f" "PI_b0ed77cfcb0fdb62" #> [1] "PI_2713ba3e" "PI_383a552e" #> [1] "pi_2713ba3e1fcb5c01" "pi_383a552e8b600d2f" #> [1] "Plefraison"  "Jiefreaford"  # Random tokens kept in a mapping file need no key. Here the file goes in a # temporary directory; in real use leave secrets_path at its default. mapping <- file.path(tempdir(), "pi_mapping_example.json") anonymize_pi(c("Franklin", "Taylor", "Franklin"), method = "token", secrets_path = mapping) #> [1] "PI_25cc31cfa269f7a2" "PI_fb852579f8ea577e" "PI_25cc31cfa269f7a2" unlink(mapping)

text: **Tests intervals.** predictor, `importance` mean, subjects bag patches without , excess IPCW integrated Brier loss left . `p_value` one-sided z test `importance > 0`, upper tail standard normal `statistic`, `p_adjusted` adjusts one-sided p-values `p_adjust`. `conf_low` `conf_high` two-sided interval level `1 - alpha`, adjusted multiple testing. p-values interval therefore answer different questions: interval excludes 0 unadjusted one-sided p-value `alpha / 2`, whereas `p_adjusted < alpha` one-sided, adjusted criterion. (`p_adjust = "none"`, predictor whose `p_value` `alpha / 2` `alpha` passes test interval still contains 0.) [autoplot()][autoplot.cbe_loco_mp_coxnet] colours predictor "Significant" `p_adjusted < alpha`, , one-sided adjusted test, whether interval excludes 0. **Data.** predictors must numeric, complete, finite, must least 3 : minipatch keeps 2 leaves least 1 . checked patch fit. minipatch fails anyway (example, one whose sampled subjects events) dropped warning gives count first error; `B` result number succeeded.

title: Institutional Categorical Hypothesis Test for gtsummary and Batch Testing — cbe_test_categorical
text: function follows rigorous 4-rule hierarchy: 2x2 table zero cell: Uses Central Fisher's exact test     mid-p adjustment (exact2x2 midp = TRUE)     avoid extreme conservatism. 2x2 table without zero cell: Uses Central Fisher's exact test     (exact2x2 midp = FALSE). RxC table sparse counts: expected cell count     less 5, runs Fisher's exact test Monte Carlo simulation     (fisher.test simulate.p.value = TRUE). RxC table adequate counts: expected cell counts     least 5, runs Pearson's Chi-squared test without continuity correction     (chisq.test correct = FALSE).

text: Generates realistic, pronounceable synthetic surnames using phonetic onsets, vowels, common surname endings (e.g., `-berg`, `-ton`, `-man`, `-wood`, `-ford`). Supports strict exclusion lists (e.g. guarantee real investigator surnames never generated) reproducible seed-based sampling without mutating global RNG state.

title: Procedural Synthetic Last Name Generator — generate_last_names
text: n Integer, number unique names generate (default 10). seed Optional integer, random seed reproducibility. exclude Character vector surnames (case-insensitive) must generated. max_tries Integer, maximum attempts multiplier throwing error distinct names generated.

title: Procedural Synthetic Last Name Generator — generate_last_names
text: character vector length `n` containing synthetic surnames.

title: Procedural Synthetic Last Name Generator — generate_last_names

Prefer environment variable writing key script. n_chars Integer, number hex characters hash digest include (default 16). Can shortened (e.g. 4 8) produce compact tokens, cost collisions different names. rename_fn Optional function transform rename tokens (e.g., tolower, toupper, custom function function(tok) paste0("INV-", substr(tok, 4, 8))). seed Optional integer, random seed reproducible random token generation name NULL. Seeded tokens derived seed alone, anyone knows can regenerate ; use secrecy matters. allow_default_key Logical, default FALSE. TRUE key available, use package's public built-key instead stopping, warn tokens secret. reproduces output made without key earlier versions; use data intend protect. allow_collisions Logical, default FALSE. TRUE, suppresses errors n_chars < 6 distinct input names map identical pseudonym tokens.

title: Integrated Brier Score of a Penalized Cox Model on Start/Stop Survival Data — glmnet_IBS
code: # \donttest{ if (requireNamespace("glmnet", quietly = TRUE) &&     requireNamespace("yardstick", quietly = TRUE) &&     requireNamespace("rsample", quietly = TRUE)) {   set.seed(1)   # Synthetic start/stop data: 60 subjects, up to 3 intervals each   long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:60, function(i) {     k <- sample(1:3, 1)     stops <- c(5, 10, 20)[1:k]     risk <- rnorm(1)     data.frame(subject_id = i, tstart = c(0, head(stops, -1)), tstop = stops,                status = c(rep(0, k - 1), rbinom(1, 1, plogis(risk))),                x1 = risk + rnorm(k, sd = 0.2), x2 = rnorm(k))   }))   rec <- recipes::recipe(~ ., data = long) |>     recipes::update_role(subject_id, tstart, tstop, status, new_role = "id variable") |>     recipes::step_range(recipes::all_numeric_predictors())   split <- rsample::group_initial_split(long, group = subject_id)   glmnet_IBS(split, alpha = 0.5, recipe = rec, feature_names = c("x1", "x2"),              time_data = unique(long[, c("tstart", "tstop")]), internal_folds = 3,              id_col = "subject_id", cox.ties = "breslow") } #> # A tibble: 2 × 5 #>     IBS lambda term  estimate alpha #>   <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>    <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 0.112 0.0746 x1           0   0.5 #> 2 0.112 0.0746 x2           0   0.5 # }

what: Security & Hardening: Pseudonym Generation and Atomic File Locking (R/pi_anonymizer.R, R/atomic_io.R)
title: TempleCBE 0.5.0
text: Audit packet A4 A5 findings identifier pseudonymization, secrets containment, atomic concurrency: Deterministic surname RNG pinning (A4-01): generate_last_names() anonymize_pi(method = "hmac_surname") now pin .rng_kind = "Mersenne-Twister", .rng_normal_kind = "Inversion", .rng_sample_kind = "Rejection" withr::with_seed (falling back), guaranteeing identical surnames regardless user worker RNGkind() R version. Pseudonym collision detection token length enforcement (A4-02): generate_pseudonym_token() now enforces n_chars >= 6 (stopping shorter lengths unless allow_collisions = TRUE), computes birthday bound collision probability warnings > 1%, validates uniqueness among distinct input names within call, failing informative collision count unless allow_collisions = TRUE. Surnames method = "hmac_surname" enforce collision checks. Empty string whitespace handling (A4-11): anonymize_pi() generate_pseudonym_token() treat empty strings "" whitespace-strings NA_character_, consistent across methods. Encoding & normalization (A4-09): Names keys normalized UTF-8 via enc2utf8() hashing. anonymize_pi() adds opt-normalize = TRUE parameter case-folding trimming prior hashing. Bounded token generation (A4-10): Capped collision resolution loops 100 attempts anonymize_pi(method = "token"), preventing infinite loops hanging file locks token entropy exhausted. Strict jsonlite requirement (A4-12): Removed fragile regex-based JSON fallbacks; method = "token" strictly requires jsonlite atomic serialization. Weak key warnings (A4-19): resolve_hmac_key() emits clear warning nchar(trimws(key)) < 16 unless allow_default_key = TRUE. Lock owner liveness atomic cleanup (A5-16): with_file_lock() records lock owner PID, verifies process liveness via non-destructive priority querying (tools::psnice()) declaring stale locks, cleans expired locks via atomic directory renaming eliminate race conditions concurrent waiters. Secrets directory validation repository containment (A5-21, A5-24): validate_secrets_dir() requires trailing slashes repo root prefix comparisons (preventing false containment positives sibling directories), verifies target existing file, verifies POSIX file modes. validate_executable() rejects directories.

title: TempleCBE 0.1.4
text: pca_percent_var_explained(): tightened top margin variance bars adding expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.01)) percent--variance y scale.

title: TempleCBE 0.1.3
text: by_column mode now respects row_order argument: row_order = FALSE (default), groups (x-axis) features (y-axis) ordered descending total missingness, matching ordering already applied default per-row/column view. Previously features stayed whatever order pivot_longer() produced (alphabetical), ignoring row_order entirely. by_column mode now auto-detects aggregated missingness effectively binary – .e. every group one contributing row (checked actual group sizes via dplyr::n(), just resulting sums) – case renders discrete “Missing”/“Present” two-level fill “Data Status” legend used default view, instead continuous black--red “# missing” gradient misleading every value 0 1 (e.g. by_column set unique subject/site id one row per group). Groups one contributing row keep existing continuous gradient, since real count meaningful (e.g. multiple readings per site time). Added fill = c("auto", "binary", "count") argument missmap() override auto-detected fill behavior explicitly needed.

title: TempleCBE 0.1.2
text: is_poisson(): chi-squared branch’s distribution.test flag inverted relative every test package (p < 0.1 mislabeled “looks Poisson”), test used statistically invalid cross-tabulation instead real goodness--fit comparison. Replaced proper chi-squared goodness--fit test using quantile-based binning fitted Poisson distribution, degrees freedom correctly reduced estimated rate. Dropped accompanying Kolmogorov-Smirnov test: KS assumes continuous null distribution, Poisson’s real point masses inflate KS statistic regardless true fit. is_normal(): switched comparing freshly simulated random sample (non-deterministic, added unnecessary noise) one-sample KS test fitted normal CDF directly. glmnet_IBS(): per-time-point Brier score normalized sum IPCW weights happened contribute, instead full test-set size — double-counted effect exclusions inflated score. Fixed follow Graf et al. (1999) IPCW estimator exactly; refactored standalone, independently-tested helpers. single_t_test(): paired = TRUE crashed unconditionally (broom::tidy() doesn’t return estimate1/estimate2 paired test) — fold-change now computed directly group vectors. Also added optional .id argument pair observations subject/record identifier instead row order, previously silently mismatched pairs unless two groups pre-sorted identically.

title: TempleCBE 0.1.2
text: ncp never passed FactoMineR::FAMD(), every fit silently capped FactoMineR’s default 5 components regardless num_comp. threshold (cumulative-variance component selection) documented tunable effect; now implemented. options (extra arguments FactoMineR::FAMD()) documented never forwarded; now implemented. print.step_famd() always printed empty column list due incorrect names() call; now uses recipes::print_step() like recipe steps. tidy.step_famd() returned fabricated placeholder values (value = 1.0, component = "PC1" every term) instead real per-component loadings/contributions. bake.step_famd() silently returned data unchanged FactoMineR became unavailable prep(); now errors clear message. Added clear error step_famd() given quantitative qualitative columns (FAMD requires mixed data).
